episode_thesis: J8 Capital's Tilman argues that a systematic futures programme should be built by decomposing return drivers into simple single-purpose sub-strategies (commodity, currency and bond trend; curve arbitrage; FX carry; inventory; volatility term structure), weighted by inverse realised volatility and scaled to a 10% target volatility, because diversification across models adds a free diversification gain and keeps the source of returns transparent. Vishal adds the Redwood intraday strategy (breakouts in volatility terms, 12 liquid futures including equity indices) as a return driver with near-zero correlation to CTA indices, while host Moritz Seibert presses on the roughly 10% a year execution-cost hurdle that such short-term trading must overcome.

speakers.name: Tilman
speakers.role: Co-founder of J8 Capital Management (London systematic hedge fund; Global Absolute Return strategy live since January 2015); civil engineer by training with a PhD in project-finance risk; formerly structured derivatives (Parkplace, UBS, AIG Financial Products, Dow Jones-AIG Commodity Index)
speakers.speaker_note: Auto-captions garble names ('Tilman saxs', 'Morits seber'); the surname is not given reliably. Referred to as Tilman (J8 co-founder). Two of the ledger's speaker labels for Moritz's questions were fixed per its corrections.

worldview_premises.premise: Translating economic fundamentals in commodities into rules-based strategies removes the emotional and behavioural biases of discretionary traders.
worldview_premises.support: His experience building the Dow Jones-AIG commodity index and rules-based strategies.

worldview_premises.premise: Besides diversification across asset classes, one can diversify across return drivers and models, and weighting signals by risk gives an additional diversification boost ('no free lunch other than diversification').
worldview_premises.support: Appeal to Fama and French's no-free-lunch view (caption garbled); no data.

worldview_premises.premise: Decomposing returns into one sub-strategy per return driver, then combining them in a risk-based portfolio, is better than one big model with filters because it keeps transparency on where returns come from and lets each driver be refined separately.
worldview_premises.support: Design argument; contrast with how 'many CTAs' build trend models with filters.

worldview_premises.premise: Each sub-strategy should have a single degree of freedom and simple parameters: the product is complex but its parts are simple.
worldview_premises.support: Design choice.

worldview_premises.premise: Equity indices have survival bias (losers drop out), which truncates the signal that a trend follower wants to carry through the whole economic cycle of an underlying; equities also depend on rates, FX and commodity inputs already traded, so adding equity trend duplicates exposure.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from index construction; adding equity index futures did not improve J8's long-term trend programme in tests.

worldview_premises.premise: Commodities have clear supply and demand fundamentals, while shares are mainly speculative instruments once issued.
worldview_premises.support: Economic argument.

worldview_premises.premise: The equity exclusion applies to the slow trend programme only; equity index futures make sense when traded differently (as in Redwood), so the redundancy argument is horizon-specific.
worldview_premises.support: He defers to Vishal's short-term system.

worldview_premises.premise: A short-term momentum strategy hedges the long-term trend programme's drawdowns during reversals.
worldview_premises.support: Design intent; his recently added cross-asset short-term momentum.

worldview_premises.premise: Two styles of carry/arbitrage: arbitraging time along a futures curve (commodity and volatility term structure) versus arbitraging between markets (FX carry, commodity inventory/curvature selection).
worldview_premises.support: Conceptual taxonomy.

worldview_premises.premise: Futures curve shape is a real-time proxy for inventory because inventory data is delayed, revised and imprecise; curvature indicates under- or oversupply, so go long undersupplied and short oversupplied commodities.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from curve shape; no test shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Rolling front-month VIX futures loses about 50-60% a year in roll costs; shorting it arbitrages the roll out, but the short has catastrophic tail risk in spikes (for example a 300% jump) and must be hedged and managed. J8 trades a relative-value trade on the VIX/VSTOXX futures term structure rather than outright short volatility.
worldview_premises.support: Long-run behaviour of rolling front-month VIX futures; the figure is from his recollection.

worldview_premises.premise: Realised volatility is stable over time while correlations and recent performance are unstable, so allocate by inverse realised volatility (equal risk) and use no correlation or performance tilts; this gave the most stable overall return.
worldview_premises.support: J8's own testing; no figures shown.

worldview_premises.premise: Combining many uncorrelated sub-strategies lowers portfolio volatility, and because futures are unfunded, exposure can be levered up to restore the 10% target volatility, converting diversification into return; realised volatility was 10.26% over 10 years, and margin is about 6-12% of equity.
worldview_premises.support: Own realised volatility over ten years; 1 million cash controls about 30 million of notional.

worldview_premises.premise: A simple index built from survey answers (about 120 replies over three years from brokers, CTAs, consultants and investors) explained about 80% of CTA index returns: a diversified, risk-weighted 12-month momentum portfolio. J8 sees itself as half traditional CTA and half alternative risk premia, so no single benchmark fits.
worldview_premises.support: His own surveys at J8's founding; the index and the 80% figure are not shown.

worldview_premises.premise: The trend signal method is the same across commodities, currencies and bonds, with market-specific parameters.
worldview_premises.support: J8 design.

worldview_premises.premise: FX carry (long high-yield, short low-yield currencies against USD) is reversed after a sell-off signalled by short-term realised volatility.
worldview_premises.support: J8 rule.

worldview_premises.premise: J8's objective is to give investors access to systematic investing in a broad, diversified and holistic way; it would add outside traders only if they offer something it has not considered.
worldview_premises.support: Business description.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: No returns, Sharpe ratios, drawdowns or correlations are disclosed for the programme or for Redwood; the only numbers are the 10.26% realised volatility over ten years and the near-zero correlation to the short-term traders index. Redwood's evidence is simulation.

The cost arithmetic does not reconcile: 8,000 round turns x 2 contracts x $6 is about 9.6%, not 10.8%; and 700 round trips per month times 12 is 8,400. Treat 10.8% as a rough figure of about 10% a year; 'per million' is not defined (capital or notional).
Vishal says costs matter little yet gives no numbers, while the host's calculation suggests a very large drag; the two views are not reconciled.
The 80% explanatory power of the survey-based 'CTA index' is asserted without the index definition or sample period.

The 50-60% a year loss from rolling VIX futures and the survival-bias argument for equities are stated as facts without data; the survival-bias argument also applies to commodity index constituents of the benchmark indices only weakly.
Tilman says adding equity index futures 'did not improve' the long-term programme while giving three a priori reasons for excluding them; the test results are not shown.
Ledger attribution fixes applied: the near-zero correlation answer (C08-4) is Vishal's; the cost arithmetic (C10-1) is the host's and is only approximate.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The speakers give almost no forward-looking market inputs. Inputs their rules use: futures curve shape (slope and curvature) as an inventory and carry signal; short-term realised volatility as the trigger to reverse FX carry; realised volatility of each sub-strategy for weights and the 10% target; intraday volatility-scaled breakouts in a trend, volatility and positioning context. Horizon ranges from hours to days (Redwood) to 12-month momentum (slow programme).
reader_inferences: (reader) The 'decomposition' design implies that each sleeve should be separately testable; a replication or adoption study could check whether the equal-risk combination beats each sleeve and a single filtered model, which J8 does not show.

(reader) The claim that realised volatility is stable while correlations are not is the key assumption behind inverse-volatility weights and the 10% target; it is testable on sleeve returns, especially around volatility spikes.

(reader) The cost-hurdle exchange implies that net-of-cost Sharpe of an intraday strategy depends on turnover per unit of capital, so capital-based and notional-based 'per million' definitions give different drags.

(reader) Tilman's reasons for excluding equities (survival bias, redundancy, speculative nature) rest on structure rather than evidence; a test of equity trend after controlling for rates, FX and commodity trends could check the redundancy claim.
